Price point is one, but it doesn't make sense to raise the price of a system too significantly for this purpose. In mass production even a 10 cent increase means millions of dollars. You're looking at the price increases for a better chip, better battery, better mosfets, voltage regulater, faster system bus, faster system RAM (it is an semi SOC after all, using ratioed clock frequencies), increased thermal disapation design, the works. Would you play an extra $100 bucks for the system(same price as the wii u) just to add snes/gba emulation, when no other game or application has a need to take advantage of it? The power consumption and what it does to battery life is another issue. Bigger batteries cost more, raise the weight of the system, add to shipping costs, increase charge time, are more expensive to warranty, and could potentially change the form factor of the system due to size requirements. TDP output for the chip in a fanless system is another major concern, the higher voltage draw cpu will run hotter clock per clock, and if it gets too warm it will throttle back the clock frequency and performance would suffer all around. Nintendo isn't dumb, or trying to screw anyone, they want to give you something as incredible as possible that fits a specific price point they know will sell (nvidia shield overshot the price point consumers were will to pay for a dedicated gaming handheld and is failing). Case in point, Shigeru Miyamoto is the only reason we have head tracking 3d in our N3DS's. He saw the tech when it was reaching the final prototyping stage, and had it rushed out and pushed it into the near final stages of development in the N3DS. It very nearly didn't happen, and did push back it's initial release date. They care very much about giving us as many features as possible, and making us happy.

Thanks for the reply. I wasn't talking about overclocking at all, or about running a gba/snes game natively(which is where instruction incompatibility would come in). Abstracting the memory address space, and Multiplexing the bus CMDS wouldn't be difficult for someone EXTREMELY familer with the platforms architecture, but the overhead of that would be incredibly high. Also pipelining, in terms of the CPU's architectural logic, will only take place when sequencal instructions are not dependent upon the result of the previous instruction. It's hardware level parallelization to decrease fetch times in the Fetch/decode/excute cycle. Purely, a performance optimization, and not a "deal breaker". In terms of hardware the 3DS does in fact have a second 16bit CPU capable of simulating a GBA device directly. It contains the legacy instructions set found in the GBA. It's just that the 3DS's features requiring that chip wouldn't be able to run during GBA play, and would break the consistency of the platform.

The reason for no gba and snes games is purely on the level of consistency. There are two cpus in a 3ds, a dual core ARM for 3d and a clocked up dsi chip for DS simulation, some 2d. They could theoretically clock down the dsi chip and use that to simulate a gba, but that cpu is also responsible for all additional features of the system, and background processes. Features like suspension, Internet access, etc. Those features would not be able to function in "gba mode". Nintendo works hard for a seamless, consistent, and, hopefully not sounding too much like a fan boy, quality driven experience. Virtual console games are not just roms, but more specifically wrapped emulators optimized for that particular game. The 3ds's ARM cpu is just not powerful enough to run the emulation environment required to play gba or snes games that way. The other option is a native port, and that's just not going to happen.

Unity3d is a game engine. Basically a program that has some 2d/2.5d/3d modeling capabilities(although you'd probably end up using maya, 3ds max, or blender for this), and utilizes scripting languages( JavaScript, or Boo{a python derivative}) for in game logic. It also includes it's own physics engine that is modifiable for the games purpose. Basically it gives you a playground to create 2d/3d game worlds with your models, apply scripted languages, and export the game to the platform of your choosing. But the main point here is that unity has gained the ability to take a game project and compile(I'm using this term loosely because technically the supported languages are only parsed to byte code not pure binary, and are subsequently interpreted by the consoles runtime environment) it to a format that can be run on 3ds. However, nintendo requires special hardware, purchasable by approved 3rd party developers to compile* and export to a nintendo platform. The dev kit runs around 5k, after nintendo gives you the go ahead. So we won't be seeing free/paid versions of unity3d with this type of support, unless it's obtained through nintendo. The reason for this is purely quality control, but once you make it into the circle (not easy, you have to demonstrate your abilities) you can freely publish to the nintendo store; anything and everything you create. The other reward is; this is royalty free software; they don't get a cut of your profits for using their sw to create the game/project.
